industry: Vertical SaaS (inspection software for environmental consultancies)

profile.story: Fieldnote is a field-inspection and reporting tool for small environmental consultancies — the firms that do phase-one site assessments, wetland delineations and stormwater inspections. Kevin wrote the first version himself in 2021 after a decade as a consultant, and at $900K ARR across 145 customers it is a real, growing, profitable software company with a proper product analytics stack, a documented onboarding and clean unit economics. It also has exactly one engineer, and he is the founder. Everything that is strong about this business — the tooling, the metrics, the automation — makes the single-point risk more conspicuous rather than less: if Kevin stops writing code, the roadmap stops that day and the support escalation path ends nowhere.

blockNotes.b1: Q8 belief is exactly right and unusually precise: the only engineer is the founder, and every other system in the business is strong enough to make that visible. Objective is scale, blocked on one hire he is afraid of getting wrong.
blockNotes.b2: Funnel built from the CRM: 30 demos a month, 22% close, $4,900 first-year value. That multiplies to about $388K of new-business value a year against $900K of ARR — roughly 43%, which the funnel cross-check will read as a mismatch and flag. It is not one. In a business where 95% of revenue is contracted and renews, new bookings are supposed to be a fraction of total revenue; the check compares new-business flow to total revenue and has no way to see the renewing base. Recorded here so the reviewer reads the flag as a model artefact and not as a number to chase. The reconciliation that does hold: 145 accounts × $6,200 average annual value = $899K.
blockNotes.b3: Price list on file with a written discount grid, last moved 2023. Cost to serve per account is in the monthly review and the heavy-imagery accounts are visible by name — the best margin visibility in the cohort. Two years of hosting and imagery API increases have not been passed through.
blockNotes.b4: 17 h/wk repetitive on a 240-hour payroll (7%). Everything that can be automated in the commercial funnel already is, monitored, with named owners. The two that are not — support triage and onboarding migration — are the two that escalate to the founder.
blockNotes.b5: Four-week test: two weeks look normal, then engineering has stopped for a fortnight and the roadmap with it. Largest customer 17%, below the overlay threshold but material at this size. Contracts, IP and vendor agreements all written and transferable — the cleanest legal position in the cohort. Production access, the repo owner account, the bank and the app store credentials are all Kevin alone.

P2.note: Every trial, demo request and partner referral lands in the CRM and an automated scheduling sequence fires within two minutes (q24, watched in session). Dani owns every inbound demo.

assessment.owner_objective: Prepare to scale — then Reduce owner dependence, Reliable revenue growth
assessment.owner_belief: I am the only engineer. Everything else in this company works — the funnel works, the onboarding works, the numbers are clean — and all of it is sitting on one person who also has to sell the vision. I have known it since we passed fifty customers and I keep not hiring because I cannot afford to hire wrong at this size.
assessment.primary_constraint: Engineering is one person: product, every bug, every integration and every production incident run through the founder's week, so the roadmap that new revenue depends on is rate-limited by the same calendar that handles support escalations and a third of pricing conversations.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Four-week test stops engineering on day one; a hotfix shipped from holiday on day three of a five-day break; a support escalation reaching him in four minutes during the session; the support backlog owned nominally by customer success and practically by him; no incident runbook; custom report templates done 'always at night'; two named lost deals citing a missing integration.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$63K of expected operating profit in demo-stage conversion lost to a two-day human response and a founder-gated pricing conversation · ~$23K of customer-success payroll on 12 weekly hours of support triage and onboarding migration · ~364 founder hours a year on support escalation, release notes and custom templates.
assessment.constraint_fix: A first engineering hire scoped narrowly to the support-and-integration queue rather than to the roadmap, an incident runbook with a second person holding production access, and a support triage tier that resolves the common cases before they reach him.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Raise plan prices for the first time since 2023 on the two-year-old price list — the discount grid is already written, gross margin is documented at 82%, and the decision is entirely his.

opportunities.title: Close more demos by removing the founder from the pricing conversation
opportunities.finding: 30 demos a month at a 22% close on $4,900 first-year value — about $1.76M of first-year value moving through the funnel annually (CRM, walked in session). Two things are demonstrably costing conversion: the first human contact is up to two business days after an automated reply that fires in two minutes, and the pricing conversation escalates to Kevin in about a third of deals (q25). Both are fixable without touching the product.
opportunities.blueprint: Same-day demo slots held on the calendar, the written discount grid given to Dani as real authority with an exception threshold, and a defined path back for the 'not this quarter' prospects the sequences currently drop.

opportunities.title: Reprice the plans for the first time since 2023
opportunities.finding: The price list on file is dated 2023 with a written discount grid behind it; hosting and imagery API costs have risen twice since, and cost-to-serve per account (Doc) shows exactly which accounts absorb that. Gross margin is documented at 82%, so a price move flows almost entirely to contribution — and with NRR at 112% and 89% logo retention, the base has demonstrated it absorbs change.
opportunities.blueprint: New list price on all new business immediately, existing accounts moved at their renewal date with 60 days' notice, usage allowances re-cut against the imagery cost that actually drives them, and the largest account handled personally and last.

opportunities.title: Tier support triage so tickets stop landing on the engineer
opportunities.finding: Support triage runs seven hours a week and escalates to Kevin — one escalation reached him in four minutes during the session (q44, demonstrated). The help desk, the runbook library and the analytics that would resolve most of it already exist; what is missing is a triage tier and a rule about what actually needs the engineer. These hours are dollarised because they come off the founder's engineering week and go back onto the roadmap the growth plan depends on.
opportunities.blueprint: AI-assisted first-response drafting against the existing runbook library with the human review step already in place, a written escalation rule naming the three ticket types that genuinely need engineering, and an incident runbook so the fourth type has a path that is not a phone call.
opportunities.replaces: Every hard ticket routing to the only engineer within minutes
